title: Short Stuff: Lemonade
summary: Short Stuff episode on the history of lemonade and the lemon. Josh and Chuck open with Halloween and childhood memories, then trace the lemon's hybrid origins (sour orange and citron, origin unknown) and early precursors like the medieval Egyptian drink cosh/kash Karai, and katarmazat, a sugar-and-lemon-juice drink made by the Jewish community in Cairo in at least the tenth century. They cover the first reference to a lemon tree in a tenth-century Arabic book, the seventeenth-century Paris lemonade vendors and their union, sparkling lemonade and Joseph Priestley's carbonation, and lemonade's American spread. The Temperance movement promoted lemonade as an alternative to liquor, and Lucy Hayes earned the nickname "Lemonade Lucy." The episode then covers pink lemonade's circus origin stories (Henry E. Allett's cinnamon candy version and the gross pink-tights washtub version), Dr. Kellogg's pink recipe, and the "when life gives you lemons, make lemonade" saying traced to Elbert Hubbard's obituary of Marshall Pinckney Wilder. Ends with a brief sign-off and contact info.

segments.title: Opening banter and Halloween
segments.summary: Josh, Chuck, and Jerry banter about childhood lemonade memories and Halloween, then introduce the episode topic: the origins of lemonade and the lemon.

segments.title: Lemon origins and medieval Egyptian precursors
segments.summary: The lemon is a human-made hybrid of a sour orange and a citron, with unknown origin. Citrons lack juice. The hosts describe cosh/kash Karai, a medieval Egyptian fermented barley drink with mint, rue, black pepper and citron leaf, and mention Chuck's and Josh's enthusiasm for fermented foods.

segments.title: Katarmazat and early lemon trees
segments.summary: Katarmazat, a tenth-century lemonade-like drink of sugar and lemon juice made by the Jewish community in Cairo, is described. Honey was likely used earlier. The first reference to a lemon tree appears in a tenth-century Arabic agricultural book, and lemons reached Italy after that.

segments.title: Paris, sparkling lemonade and the lemonade union
segments.summary: Modern lemonade is traced to seventeenth-century Paris, where a sparkling lemon-honey drink debuted. Street vendors sold it from tanks on their backs, it spread across Europe, and vendors formed a union in 1676. Joseph Priestley's carbonation invention, and Schweppes' work in the 1780s, made lemonade fizzy. Hosts discuss sugary lemon sodas.

segments.title: Temperance movement and Lemonade Lucy
segments.summary: Lemonade spread across America and was promoted by the Temperance movement as an alternative to liquor. Rutherford B. Hayes' White House banned liquor, and his wife Lucy Hayes was nicknamed Lemonade Lucy.

segments.title: Pink lemonade and circus origin stories
segments.summary: Pink lemonade is linked to the circus, with an 1879 Wheeling Register story. Henry E. Allett's cinnamon-candy story (from a 1912 New York Times obituary) and a gross pink-tights washtub story from 1957 are discussed. Dr. Kellogg's cranberry or grenadine recipe is also mentioned.

segments.title: When life gives you lemons: Marshall Pinckney Wilder
segments.summary: The saying 'make lemonade out of lemons' is traced to Elbert Hubbard's 1915 obituary of Marshall Pinckney Wilder, a three-and-a-half-foot-tall comedian who said fate handed him a lemon and he made lemonade of it.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and point listeners to the show website and email address for contact.
